2805.prule: Stress usually falls on the last (rightmost) long vowel of the word: unbounded, quantity-sensitive, right-oriented ('Ударение падает обычно на последний долгий гласный' = 'Stress usually falls on the last long vowel'). 2805.exq_: Ударение падает обычно на последний долгий гласный. ('usually'; no lexical exceptions listed)
2805.tone: §2.1.3 (p. 74): a possible link between aspiration and vowel tone in the SOUTH-EASTERN dialects (rising tone next to aspirated consonants); nothing tonal claimed for the north-western group. Edelman's Dardic overview in the same volume (p. 17): 'Место ударения варьирует по языкам, в большинстве языков оно фиксированное, тяготеет к концу слова.... В гавар, катаркалаи, кховар, башкарик, шина, диалектах пашаи (и в дамели) выявлены тоновые оппозиции, появление которых связано в значительной мере с утратой аспирации древними звонкими придыхательными. Характер и количество тонов известны не во всех языках.' (= place of stress varies by language, in most it is fixed and gravitates to the word end; tonal oppositions identified in Gawar, Katarqalai, Khowar, Bashkarik, Shina, dialects of Pashai (and Dameli), largely tied to the loss of aspiration in the old voiced aspirates). Strand's Degano page (SE Pashai, Goraik) lists primary/secondary pitch accent as phonemic without a placement rule. So for Pashai overall: a hedged quantity rule plus dialectal (SE) tone, not a tone system replacing stress.

tn.quote: 声調 (Tone) については, 本来的な有声帯気閉鎖音, たとえば, *dh を含む語 ... に対応するパシャイ語は dúm であり, 非帯気音化すると共に, 声調（この場合は上昇調）を獲得したものと考えられているが, コールダル方言に関しては, その判定が困難であって今後の調査研究が必要である。dår《山》: dår《木》(前者が上昇調, 後者が平板調あるいは下降調) の対立が存在するが, 前者が [dåˀr] なのか, [dår] と上昇調なのかの判定は目下のところ下されない。 ... pən《泡》tar-《見る》, についても同様で, 上昇調で発音されるか否か不明である。
tn.translation: As for tone: the Pashai word corresponding to words with an original voiced aspirated stop, e.g. *dh ..., is dúm, and it is thought that together with de-aspiration it acquired tone (here a rising tone); but for the Kordar dialect that judgement is difficult and further investigation is needed. An opposition dår 'mountain': dår 'wood' exists (the former rising, the latter level or falling), but whether the former is [dåˀr] or [dår] with rising tone cannot at present be decided. ... The same holds for pən 'foam', tar- 'see': whether they are pronounced with rising tone is unclear.

tn.note: Nawata hears a possible rising vs level/falling contrast (dår 'mountain' vs dår 'wood') tied to lost aspiration, but cannot rule out glottalization [dåˀr] and leaves Kordar tone unresolved.

Stated as a preliminary account ('appears to be weight sensitive').

2810.heavy: not applicable: vowel length is itself the lexically specified accent, not a conditioning weight; the source gives no weight-to-stress rule
2810.prule: Philippine-type contrastive accent realised as phonemic vowel length, not loudness: each root lexically has either a long or a short penultimate vowel (minimal pairs salug 'floor' vs sa:lug 'river'); length is confined to non-final vowels followed by a single consonant, is never distinctive on the word-final vowel, and (in inherited words) never precedes a consonant cluster. 'Stress, or loudness' is explicitly non-distinctive. No positional stress rule is given; the accent is lexically arbitrary.
2810.srule: Not mentioned in McFarland 1974, Ch. 2 'Phonology' (pp. 31, 41-42) or the Northern Catanduanes length passages (pp. 194, 196-197); the source denies distinctive stress altogether and describes only lexical vowel length.
2810.quote: Vowel length is distinctive in all Bikol area dialects, but stress, or loudness, is not. Length is non-distinctive after the final vowel of a word. In inherited words, length does not occur before a consonant cluster. 2813.dq: As reported in Chapter Two, the root of a verb stem usually bears the stress. Aside from this general observation, I have not yet worked out all the realizations of stress and pitch accent at the word, phrase and sentence level in sufficient detail to be able to include transcriptions of prosodic phenomena here.
2813.prule: Stress/accent is borne by the verb root: 'the root of a verb stem usually bears the stress' (p. 9 fn. 4); 'The root typically carries the accent' (p. 20). The root is a CV morpheme that follows an optional CV- instrumental prefix (ma-bah, pha-bah), so the stressed syllable is fixed by morphological structure, not by syllable count. Framed within Vihman's (1976:77) analysis, adopted by O'Connor, that 'stress is an inherent lexical feature' and pitch a phonetic correlate of syllable structure (long vowels carry low pitch; unaccented vowels are laxed; amplitude reported as a stress cue).

Later Pomoan stress surveys (Buckley 2014/2019/2020) likewise give no secondary-stress statement for Northern Pomo.

2814.prule: Stress is predictable and non-contrastive: it falls on the lexical root syllable of the word (the root is monosyllabic 'with one exception'); person/number prefixes are pre-tonic and dual/plural suffixes and the second vowel of VhV/VʔV roots are post-tonic. 2814.tone: Two contrastive tones, high and rising (Berthiaume 2012; Avelino 1997/2002 posit three: alto, bajo, descendente), contrastive only on the stressed root syllable; 'fundamentally a pitch-accent system' (Berthiaume 2012:33). tn.quote: Northern Pame has two contrastive tones, which are a high tone and a rising tone. Tone is contrastive on the lexical root, which is also the location of stress. ... Thus, identical to other Pame descriptions (Avelino 1997, 2002, Gibson and Bartholomew 1979, Gibson 1956 and Manrique 1967) the present research describes tone as fundamentally a pitch-accent system. ... tone is only contrastive on the lexical (and stressed) root, which with one exception, is always monosyllabic. Pitch variations on non-root syllables can always be determined by the pitch of the root syllable.
tn.cite: Berthiaume, Scott Charles. 2012. A Phonological Grammar of Northern Pame. SIL e-Books 37. Dallas: SIL International. ix+134 pp. ISBN 978-1-55671-307-1 (published version of the 2003 University of Texas at Arlington PhD dissertation).

2815.tone: Sande 2015 describes Nouchi as a tone language: lexical tone on every word including monosyllables, plus productive grammatical tone; the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prosody', 'intonation' and 'pitch' do not occur anywhere in the paper (full-text search), so the paper makes no stress statement at all. Competing position, read in the copy consulted: Boutin & Kouadio N'Guessan 2015 (HAL hal-01408710) dispute that the tonal system is Nouchi-specific and hold that nouchi and français populaire ivoirien have 'le même système phonologique et prosodique', the tones and 'la tendance à une accentuation de mots au lieu d'une accentuation syntagmatique' having already been documented for Ivorian French. Their evidence is Boutin & Turcsan 2009 §4.4.7, which describes Ivorian French, not Nouchi: 'L'accentuation, en français de Côte d'Ivoire, tend à séparer, davantage qu'en français standard, les mots d'un même syntagme et ne porte pas toujours sur la dernière syllabe du syntagme ou du mot' (numerals and 'un' accented; ordinals and acronyms accented on their first syllable; some homophone pairs distinguished by a high tone), and §4.4.8 'l'accent initial, y compris celui des clitiques'. Ahua 2007 §3.6 and Ahua 2008 §2.3 use 'accentuation' only for emphatic lengthening that marks degree ('tient lieu de marque de degré, comme dans les langues africaines'); Ahua 2008's conclusion says Nouchi prosody still awaits a dedicated study. Both camps agree tone is present; no source…

2816.prule: Every word/foot has one accented syllable, cued by length (and full vowel quality per Cox apud Dakubu), not intensity; accent position is not fixed by syllable count ('contrasts between a foot with stress on the first syllable with a foot with stress on the second syllable') and is 'grammatically determined' (Dakubu 1981: 235 reporting Cox 1974: 25). 2817.tone: Mamet keeps two 'accents' apart: 'accent de hauteur' = tone (H marked by acute, unmarked vowel = L, rising and falling contours) and 'accent d'intensité' = stress, which he calls weak ('doit être rendu sans exagération'). The modern sketches of both varieties (Bakamba Mputu 2004, Inongo; Motingea 2010 ch. 5, Bikoro) describe a two-tone system with lexical and grammatical tone and say nothing about stress. Gilliard 1928 (Inongo) uses 'accent' only for tense-marking melodies (p. 23 'L'accent est sur l'antépénultième: té'; 'L'accent tombant sur le verbe, il prend un sens de passé'), not for a word-stress rule.

Heavy = syllable closed by a coda cluster, or by a continuant, tap, lateral or hetero-organic nasal ('Syllables closed by coda clusters, continuants, taps, laterals, and hetero-organic nasals attract stress', p.36). Not heavy: syllables closed by a homorganic nasal (0/6 trisyllables penult), by the first half of a geminate (0/5), or, mostly, by a hetero-organic stop (2/12). 2820.dflt: Initial syllable of the domain: all disyllables and most trisyllables initial (grid 10, 100); quadrisyllables secondary on 1st and primary on 3rd (1010 with primary on syllable 3); verbs: first syllable of the root plus every alternate syllable, never the final syllable, last stress primary.
2820.prule: Trochaic feet aligned from the left edge of each polysyllabic morpheme (the stress domain; monosyllabic/consonantal suffixes join the preceding domain); final syllables are never stressed; where a word has more than one stress the final (rightmost) stress is primary. Heavy syllables, i.e. syllables closed by a coda cluster or by a continuant, tap, lateral or hetero-organic nasal, attract stress: trisyllables with a heavy second syllable take penultimate stress, verbs shift stress off the root-initial syllable onto such a syllable. Otherwise: disyllables initial, trisyllables initial, quadrisyllables secondary on 1st and primary on 3rd.
2820.srule: All non-final stresses of a multiply-stressed word are secondary (the rightmost stress is primary; no secondary/tertiary ranking). They fall by the same left-aligned trochaic parse: root/domain-initial syllable and every alternate syllable after it, never the final syllable (quadrisyllables: secondary on 1st, primary on 3rd). Polysyllabic prefix complexes: secondary stress on their initial syllable; a monosyllabic prefix complex bears a secondary stress only when stress is not on the root-initial syllable. Disyllabic word-level suffixes: secondary stress on their initial syllable; monosyllabic =ji, =mirl, =wany unstressed except =wany before =mirl.

2821.tone: Two-tone language (high, low) plus downstep; 'tone is primarily used to encode lexical contrasts'; Clark (1990) analyses H as underspecified and downstep as arising from a sequence of two high tones (incl. a floating associative H); focus/topic marked by particles and word order, not by prominence-lending pitch events. No canonical stress correlates ('neither of these languages displays typical acoustic correlates of lexical stress, such as increased vowel duration or intensity'); word-level metrical prominence is inferred only from downstep resistance of trisyllabic nouns (Clark 1990, carried second-hand) and from co-speech-gesture apex alignment (word-final default, probabilistic, 4 speakers). The source treats this as metrical structure, never as stress or pitch accent. Corroboration (Ikekeonwu 1991 JIPA, pp. 100-101, first-hand, Standard Igbo; re-read by C): 'Two distinctive tones are often recognized in Igbo; in addition, there is a third tone, a downstepped high.'... 'There is the tonal phenomenon of downdrift in Igbo: each succeeding high tone is lower than the preceding one, especially when there is an intervening low tone. In a sequence H - L - H, the second high is on a lower pitch than the first. Low tones are also affected by downdrift. This phenomenon, of course, is of no phonemic significance.' The Conventions section says nothing about stress or accent (the word does not occur in).

2824.heavy: Heavy = a closed syllable and/or a syllable containing a 'tense' vowel (ɔ, i, u). Ultima counts only if closed AND tense-vowelled; penult counts if closed OR tense-vowelled. Source on the vowels (2019, p. 686): 'The vowels are distinguished by quality rather than quantity. Three of the principle vowels, the ‘tense’ vowels ɔ, i and u, are lengthened in open accented syllables to [ɔː] or [ɒː], [iː] and [uː]. These normally represent the reflexes of the PS series of long vowels... The other three principle vowels, the ‘lax’ vowels a, e and o, appear only exceptionally in open accented syllables.'
2824.dflt: Final syllable when no syllable qualifies: dəmɔ́ ‘blood’, bəġásˁ ‘he stopped’ (2019); qamɔ́ ‘before’, əháw ‘he gave’ (2025). In words of three or more syllables the 2019 text sends stress to the antepenult 'if neither the ultima nor the penultima is closed and contains a tense vowel' (gatˁél-nɔ-χon); read literally, with that clause overriding the penult clause, it mispredicts the author's own p. 686 transcriptions qanɔjɔ [qaˈnɔːjɔ] ‘smith’ and moʃmenɔnɔ [mʌʃ.mɛ.ˈnɔː.nɔ] ‘Muslims’ (3 and 4 syllables, open tense penult stressed), so the penult clause (closed OR tense) applies at all word lengths and the antepenult clause is the residual case (penult neither closed nor tense). gatˁélnɔχon (open tense penult nɔ unstressed) is the one cited example the condensed rule does not derive, presumably because -nɔ-χon are suffix/enclitic material (§4.4.2: suffixation 'may also cause the accent to shift'). The 2025 wording (antepenult in 3+-syllable words 'provided that either syllable is closed or contains a tense vowel', else final) likewise mispredicts qanɔ́jɔ and moʃmenɔ́nɔ.
2824.prule: Right-edge, weight-conditioned stress computed from the final syllable, as an ordered decision list: (1) a final syllable that is closed AND contains a tense vowel (ɔ, i, u) is stressed (qə=mahrəwɔ́t; 2025: Baġdɔ́d); (2) otherwise the penult is stressed if it is closed OR contains a tense vowel (kálbɔ; 2025: éṯmal, ṣɔ́tni; and the pp. 686-687 transcriptions qanɔ́jɔ 'smith', moʃmenɔ́nɔ 'Muslims', klɔ́θɔ 'three' with an open tense penult); (3) in words of three or more syllables whose penult is neither closed nor tense, stress recedes to the antepenult (the 2019 text words this as 'if neither the ultima nor the penultima is closed and contains a tense vowel', example gatˁél-nɔ-χon); (4) otherwise stress is final (dəmɔ́, bəġásˁ; 2025: qamɔ́, əháw). The 2025 restatement keeps the same order: superheavy ultima > penult in disyllables / antepenult in 3+-syllable words 'provided that either syllable is closed or contains a tense vowel' > final.

2825.dq: The stress tone lies on the stem-syllable. This is best observable in the plural of substantives, where the stem-syllable has a clearly distinguishable stress, as opposed to the pre- and suffixes.

2825.prule: Stress falls on the stem syllable; prefixes and suffixes are unstressed ('The stress tone lies on the stem-syllable... as opposed to the pre- and suffixes'). Nuer stems are predominantly monosyllabic (Reid 2019), so in affixed words this is root stress. Stated alongside lexical ('etymological') and grammatical tone.

2825.tone: Westermann 1912 §39: five tone marks (high, low, middle, high-low falling, low-high rising); 'etymological tones' distinguish words with the same segments (kót God / kòt reed); 'grammatical tone' (all personal pronouns high; past and passive verb high-low); tone sandhi in connected speech ('rhythmical intonation'); tones clearest in isolation. Modern first-hand descriptions (Reid 2019 PhD Surrey, Monich 2020 SAL 49, Gjersøe 2020 PhD Leipzig, Reid 2025 SAL 54) analyse Nuer with three tonemes /H, M, L/, three-way vowel length and phonation, and never mention stress or accent (a full-text search of the held texts: zero hits). Gjersøe 2020 sec. 1.1.1: 'Storch (2005)... adds another parameter to tone by claiming that Nuer has stress. It is not clear how tone and stress go together in her account of Nuer'; ch. 7 fn. 3: Storch annotates stem stress with an acute (second-hand; Storch 2005 not seen).

tn.quote: The tones are marked thus:—á high tone, à low tone, a̍ middle tone, â high-low (falling) tone, ǎ low-high (rising) tone.
